title: Human factors and safety culture
blurb: Explain how the job, the person and the organisation shape error, classify human failure, and build a culture where people speak up.
question: Two medicines in near-identical boxes are stored side by side. Nurses have picked the wrong one twice this month, each time spotted at the bedside check. What is the most effective response?

teach.body: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety. In plain English: people make errors because of the situations they work in as well as who they are. Designing the work around real human limits prevents more harm than telling people to try harder.

teach.body: Situational awareness is knowing what is going on around you and what may happen next; shared situational awareness is a common understanding across the team. Safety huddles and structured handovers build it. Checklists catch slips and lapses, but only if anyone can stop the process: if a check is missed, say so clearly and ask for a pause. Code standard 16 requires acting without delay on risks to patient safety, including raising and, if necessary, escalating concerns (16.1).
teach.cite: NMC Code 16, 16.1, 19.1; JESIP shared situational awareness

teach.body: A just culture treats honest error as a chance to learn: support the person, thank them for reporting and look at the system factors, as PSIRF requires. Reckless or deliberate unsafe acts are handled differently. People need to feel safe to speak up: local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians continue in trusts, although the National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026. Nurses must not obstruct or victimise anyone raising a concern (Code 16.5).
teach.cite: PSIRF; NMC Code 16; Raising concerns guidance

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pharmacy cupboard on a renal ward
teach.body: Staff Nurse Mei notices two medicines in near-identical boxes stored side by side; twice this month the wrong one was picked and caught at the bedside check. Rather than asking staff to 'be more careful', she reports both near misses, separates the boxes, adds shelf alerts and raises it with the pharmacist so the supply can be changed. This targets the job design factor; slips like these are not removed by warnings alone.

teach.text: Slip or lapse = right plan, wrong execution (fix the design). Mistake = wrong plan (fix knowledge and procedures). Violation = deliberate shortcut (find out why the rule is being bypassed). 'Remind staff to be careful' fixes none of them well.

items: Code 19.2 uses the HSE definition: environmental, organisational and job factors and individual characteristics.
Errors are slips, lapses or mistakes; violations are deliberate deviations from rules.
Design out slips and lapses; train against mistakes; fix the causes of violations.
Fatigue, distraction and time pressure raise error rates: manage them, and stay fit for your role, for example by declining unsafe extra hours (Code 20.9: maintain the health your role needs).
Anyone can stop a check; honest errors are met with support and system learning.

summary: You can now explain human factors using the HSE definition, classify slips, lapses, mistakes and violations and match each to an effective fix. You can also build shared situational awareness, speak up at the moment of risk and respond to error with a just, learning culture.

A.q: Which description of human factors does the NMC Code (19.2) use?
options: The personal mistakes that lead to disciplinary action
Job, organisational and environmental factors, and individual traits
The physical strength needed to move and handle patients
Psychological traits that make a nurse unsuitable for clinical practice
A.why: Code 19.2 cites the HSE definition: environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety.

whyNot.0: Human factors look at the whole system that shapes behaviour, not individual blame.
whyNot.2: Physical capability is one individual factor among many, not the definition.
whyNot.3: The concept is about how work and people interact, not judging suitability.

A.q: After flushing a patient's cannula, an experienced nurse forgets to restart the infusion pump, a task she does many times a day. How does the HSE classify this?
options: A mistake from a wrong plan
A deliberate routine violation
A failure of basic competence
A lapse in a familiar task
A.why: Slips and lapses are unintended actions or omissions in familiar, well-practised tasks; the plan was right but not carried out. They are best reduced by design, such as prompts and alarms (HSE).

whyNot.0: A mistake is where the intended action itself is wrong; here the plan was correct.
whyNot.1: A violation is a deliberate deviation; forgetting is not deliberate.
whyNot.2: She is experienced and competent; lapses happen to skilled people in routine tasks.

A.q: A ward's medicines rounds are interrupted on average 10 times each. Which change best targets this human factor?
options: Remind nurses at handover to concentrate
Record each interruption on the drug chart
Protect round time with a visible signal
Move the round to the busiest visiting hour of the day
A.why: Distraction is a recognised performance influencing factor. Designing the system to reduce interruptions, for example protected time and a visible do-not-disturb signal, targets the cause (HSE; Code 19.2).

whyNot.0: Exhortation does not remove the interruptions that cause errors.
whyNot.1: Recording interruptions on a drug chart does not reduce them and clutters the record.
whyNot.3: Visiting time is likely to increase interruptions.

B.q: A newly registered nurse calculates an infusion rate using a formula she believes is correct but which applies to a different type of infusion. How does the HSE classify this?
options: A slip of attention
A memory lapse
A mistake
A violation
B.why: A mistake is an error of judgement or decision-making where the intended action is wrong, often because of a gap in knowledge or a rule misapplied from a similar situation. Training on sound procedures is the main prevention (HSE).

whyNot.0: A slip is a correct plan carried out wrongly; here the plan itself was wrong.
whyNot.1: A lapse is forgetting a step; she applied the wrong rule.
whyNot.3: A violation is deliberate; she believed she was correct.

B.q: Staff on a ward routinely skip the second check for controlled drugs at night because a second registrant is rarely free. What is the best response?
options: Issue a written warning to staff who skip checks
Find out why it happens and make the check workable
Remove the second check at night to match practice
Remind staff of the policy at the next team meeting
B.why: Violations are deliberate deviations, rarely malicious, often caused by unworkable rules or resources. Finding the root cause and involving staff in a workable solution is the HSE approach.

whyNot.0: Punishment without fixing the cause is unlikely to change behaviour and discourages openness.
whyNot.2: Removing a safety check to match unsafe practice increases risk.
whyNot.3: A reminder does not address why the check cannot be done.

B.q: Before a bedside procedure, a nurse notices the safety checklist has not been completed and the doctor is about to start. What should she do?
options: Say the check is missing and ask for a pause
Complete the checklist herself afterwards
Report it on the incident system after the case
Tell the nurse in charge about it at the end of the shift
B.why: Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process. Code standard 16 requires acting without delay on risks to patient safety, so she should speak up clearly at the moment of risk, whatever her seniority.

whyNot.1: Completing it afterwards defeats its purpose and is falsifying a record.
whyNot.2: Reporting afterwards does not prevent the harm the check is designed to catch.
whyNot.3: Waiting until the end of the shift leaves the risk unaddressed.

C.q: Nadia, a healthcare assistant, reports that she gave a patient the wrong meal texture; the patient coughed but recovered. The manager learns the two patients' diet cards were swapped. What response reflects a just culture?
options: Give Nadia a formal warning to make the expected standard clear
Remove Nadia from mealtime duties until retrained
Thank and support Nadia and review how the cards got swapped
Record the error in Nadia's personnel file for review
C.why: A just culture treats honest error as a chance to learn: support the person, thank them for reporting and look at system contributors, here the swapped cards. This encourages the reporting that PSIRF and Code 14 depend on.

whyNot.0: Punishing honest error discourages reporting and ignores the system cause.
whyNot.1: Removing her from duties treats a system problem as an individual failing.
whyNot.3: A personnel record of an honest error is punitive and deters openness.

C.q: At the start of a busy shift, the nurse in charge wants every team member to know which patients are deteriorating, who is at risk of falls and where staff are short. What is the most effective approach?
options: Email the information to staff after handover
Hold a brief safety huddle on risks and plans
Rely on each nurse reading every patient's notes
Put the information in the ward diary for later
C.why: Shared situational awareness, a common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is built by short structured safety huddles where risks are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; JESIP principles).

whyNot.0: Email may not be read in time and does not allow discussion of plans.
whyNot.2: Reading every set of notes takes too long and gives no shared picture.
whyNot.3: A diary entry is passive and is unlikely to be read in time.

C.q: Two medicines in near-identical boxes are stored next to each other, and two picking errors have been caught at the bedside this month. What is the most effective response?
options: Remind staff at handover to read labels carefully
Ask the nurses involved to write reflective accounts
Add a third check to every medicine given on the ward
Report the near misses and separate the boxes
C.why: Look-alike packaging is a job design factor that causes slips. HSE notes slips cannot be eliminated by training alone; better design reduces them. Reporting the near misses and changing storage targets the cause (Code 19.1–19.2).

whyNot.0: Reminders rely on attention, which is exactly what fails in a slip.
whyNot.1: Reflection may help individuals but leaves the hazard in place.
whyNot.2: A blanket extra check adds workload and interruptions without fixing the cause.

reteach.title: Design the trap out of the room
reteach.question: If people keep tripping on the same step, do you train them to walk better or fix the step?

blocks.body: Skilled people still slip on a badly designed step, especially when tired, rushed or interrupted. Human factors thinking asks what about the job, the person and the organisation made the error likely, and changes the design: separate look-alike medicines, protect drug rounds, use checklists everyone can stop. It also asks why rules are bypassed, rather than just punishing the people who bypass them.

blocks.h: Match the failure to the fix
head: Failure
Best fix
rows: Find the reason; make the rule workable

blocks.text: A just culture is not a 'no consequences' culture: honest errors get support and system learning; reckless acts are handled differently.

explain.body: Human factors: environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety. Code 19.2 asks nurses to take account of human factors and system failures.

test.q: Which body's definition of human factors does the NMC Code quote?
options: The Health and Safety Executive
The Care Quality Commission
NHS England's patient safety team
The World Health Organization
test.why: Code 19.2 quotes the Health and Safety Executive definition of human factors.

whyNot.1: The CQC regulates providers in England but is not the source of the Code's definition.
whyNot.2: NHS England leads PSIRF and LFPSE, but the Code cites the HSE.
whyNot.3: The WHO publishes patient safety material, but the Code cites the HSE.

explain.body: Slips and lapses: unintended actions in familiar tasks (wrong button, forgotten step); reduce through design. Mistakes: the plan itself is wrong, often a knowledge gap; reduce through training on sound procedures.

test.q: Which measure is most effective against slips and lapses in a familiar task?
options: Better design and prompts
Extra theory teaching sessions
Disciplinary warnings
Longer shift patterns
test.why: Slips and lapses happen in well-practised tasks and cannot be removed by training alone; better design reduces their frequency (HSE).

whyNot.1: Teaching targets mistakes from knowledge gaps, not slips by skilled staff.
whyNot.2: Warnings do not change attention-based errors and discourage reporting.
whyNot.3: Longer shifts increase fatigue and make slips more likely.

explain.body: Violations are deliberate deviations from a rule or procedure, rarely malicious, often to save time because equipment, staffing or rules are unworkable. Find the root cause and involve staff in practical procedures.

test.q: Nurses keep propping open a fire door to move beds because the door is too heavy for one person. How is this best described?
options: A slip
A lapse
A mistake
A violation
test.why: A deliberate departure from a rule, here to cope with an unworkable door, is a violation. The fix is to address the cause, for example a door holder linked to the fire alarm (HSE).

whyNot.0: A slip is unintended; propping the door is deliberate.
whyNot.1: A lapse is a forgotten step; this is a chosen action.
whyNot.2: A mistake is a wrong plan believed to be right; staff know the rule and bypass it.

explain.body: Honest errors are met with support and system learning; reporting is thanked. Anyone can stop a process when a check is missed. Concerns go to the line manager, then a designated person such as an FTSU Guardian, then higher, then a regulator.

test.q: A nurse raised a safety concern with her manager and nothing changed. Who is an appropriate next contact within the trust?
options: The local newspaper
An FTSU Guardian
The patient's family
Her own social media followers
test.why: NMC Raising concerns guidance moves from line manager to a designated person in the organisation; local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians continue in trusts despite the National Guardian's Office closing in June 2026.

whyNot.0: Going to the media first bypasses internal and regulatory routes and loses protection.
whyNot.2: Sharing concerns with a family breaches confidentiality and does not resolve the system issue.
whyNot.3: Posting on social media breaches confidentiality and NMC social media guidance.
